question: NPC: How do you choose the right wireless technology for a site?
intro: I'm Tariq, the Beacon-Courier. A new phone and a ten-year-old smart thermostat can join the same Wi-Fi network and get very different service from it. What each one gets depends on which generation of radio it has and which bands that radio can use. The generations' names don't make that easy, so let's sort them out first.

beats.say: Wi-Fi uses **bands**, stretches of radio frequency in gigahertz (GHz).
**Wi-Fi 5** works on 5 GHz only; **Wi-Fi 6** adds 2.4 GHz.

steps.say: Wi-Fi uses **bands**, stretches of radio frequency in gigahertz (GHz). **Wi-Fi 5** works on 5 GHz only; **Wi-Fi 6** adds 2.4 GHz.

beats.say: **Wi-Fi 6E** is Wi-Fi 6 with the radio extended into 6 GHz.
**Wi-Fi 7** has channels up to 320 MHz and **multi-link operation**, which lets a device use two bands at once.

steps.say: **Wi-Fi 6E** is Wi-Fi 6 with the radio extended into 6 GHz. **Wi-Fi 7** has channels up to 320 MHz and **multi-link operation**, which lets a device use two bands at once.

check.prompt: A Wi-Fi 7 access point serves an older Wi-Fi 5 laptop. What happens?
check.answer: They connect as Wi-Fi 5, in the 5 GHz band they share
wrong: They cannot connect, because generations do not mix
They connect as Wi-Fi 7 once the AP updates the laptop
check.why: Each generation is backward compatible: a newer AP still speaks the older standards, so the pair settles on the newest standard and band they both support. The laptop gains nothing from Wi-Fi 7's features.

beats.say: Lower frequencies travel farther and pass through walls better.

beats.say: **2.4 GHz** is shared with Bluetooth and microwave ovens; 6 GHz adds 1,200 MHz of new US spectrum.
Dual-band clients often cling to 2.4 GHz. **Band steering** nudges them onto 5 or 6 GHz.

check.prompt: A smart thermostat supports 2.4 GHz only. What does band steering do to it?
check.answer: Nothing: it stays on 2.4 GHz, the only band it has
wrong: It moves the thermostat to 5 GHz for more speed
It blocks the thermostat, because steering closes 2.4 GHz
check.why: Band steering acts only on clients the AP has seen on both bands. A 2.4 GHz-only device is never pushed anywhere, and keeping 2.4 GHz uncrowded for devices like it is half the point.

In 2.4 GHz, channel centers sit 5 MHz apart but each channel is about 20 MHz wide, so neighbors overlap.

question: Aria checks how a laptop at Silverkeep Holdings is connected, using Windows. Which Wi-Fi generation is the laptop using?
code:
C:\> netsh wlan show interfaces
    Name           : Wi-Fi
    State          : connected
    Band           : 6 GHz
    Channel        : 37
    Radio type     : 802.11ax
correct: Wi-Fi 6E
incorrect: Wi-Fi 6
Wi-Fi 7
Wi-Fi 5
feedback: 802.11ax in the 6 GHz band is Wi-Fi 6E: the same 802.11ax radio extended into 6 GHz. Plain Wi-Fi 6 is also 802.11ax but stops at 2.4 and 5 GHz, so it could never report a 6 GHz band. Wi-Fi 7 would show 802.11be, and Wi-Fi 5 is 802.11ac, which works in 5 GHz only.

question: Which statements about Wi-Fi generations and bands are correct?
correct: Wi-Fi 5 (802.11ac) radios operate only in the 5 GHz band
Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be) lets one device use two bands at once
6 GHz has the most spectrum but the shortest range of the three
incorrect: Wi-Fi 6E is a separate standard, 802.11be, built for 6 GHz
Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax) radios work in the 5 and 6 GHz bands only
2.4 GHz offers more non-overlapping channels than 5 GHz
A Wi-Fi 6 laptop can join 6 GHz after a driver update
feedback: Wi-Fi 5 is 802.11ac and 5 GHz only, Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be) adds multi-link operation across bands, and 6 GHz trades range for a large block of new spectrum. Wi-Fi 6 is 802.11ax in 2.4 and 5 GHz, and Wi-Fi 6E is still 802.11ax (802.11be is Wi-Fi 7). 2.4 GHz has only three non-overlapping channels, far fewer than 5 GHz, and no driver can add a 6 GHz radio that the hardware lacks.

question: Aria must set AP-C's 2.4 GHz channel. In her survey drawing, a line joins two APs whose coverage overlaps. Which channel should AP-C use?
feedback: AP-C overlaps AP-A (channel 1) and AP-B (channel 6), so of the three clear channels only 11 is left. AP-D also uses 11, but its cell doesn't touch AP-C's, so reusing the channel there is fine. Channel 6 would put AP-C on the same channel as a neighbor, channel 3 overlaps both 1 and 6, and 36 is a 5 GHz channel that a 2.4 GHz radio can't use.

question: NPC: What do you use where Wi-Fi and cable don't reach?
intro: Some sites have no cable nearby and no Wi-Fi worth the name: a farm, a ship, a pop-up shop. Their link has to come from the sky, either through a carrier's towers or from a satellite. We'll take the towers first.

beats.say: **Cellular** service, 4G LTE or 5G, links a site through a carrier's towers, using a router with a SIM.
It is a common backup when a wired WAN fails, and the main link where no cable reaches.

steps.say: **Cellular** service, 4G LTE or 5G, links a site through a carrier's towers, using a router with a SIM. It is a common backup when a wired WAN fails, and the main link where no cable reaches.

beats.say: **Satellite** reaches places with no towers, but the dish needs a clear sky, and heavy rain weakens the signal.

beats.code:
GEO  35,786 km up
     ~600 ms delay
LEO  200-2,000 km up
     tens of ms delay

beats.say: **Geostationary (GEO)** satellites sit far higher than **low Earth orbit (LEO)** ones, so their delay is longer.

steps.say: **Satellite** reaches places with no towers, but the dish needs a clear sky, and heavy rain weakens the signal. **Geostationary (GEO)** satellites sit far higher than **low Earth orbit (LEO)** ones, so their delay is longer.

check.prompt: Light travels about 300,000 km per second. Roughly how long does one trip up to a GEO satellite and back down take?
check.answer: About 240 ms
wrong: About 24 ms
About 2.4 seconds
check.why: Up and down is about 71,600 km, and at 300,000 km per second that is about 0.24 seconds. A request and its reply each make that trip, which is why GEO round trips run past half a second.

outro: Next, a ground-floor shop in a narrow street has no view of the open sky. Choose the link that suits it.

question: Ember Forge Workshop is a ground-floor shop in a narrow street, with no view of the open sky. The owner wants an automatic backup WAN link for when its fiber fails, and the 5G phone signal inside is strong. Which backup fits?
correct: A cellular router with a 5G SIM that takes over on failure
incorrect: A LEO satellite dish mounted inside the shop's front window
A GEO satellite dish bolted to the shop's front wall
A second fiber line, run through the same street duct
feedback: Cellular fits: strong 5G is already there, a cellular router can fail over automatically, and it needs no view of the sky. Any satellite dish, LEO or GEO, needs a clear view of the sky, which this shop lacks, and GEO would add over half a second to every round trip as well. A second fiber in the same duct shares the first one's path, so one cut takes both down.

question: A remote site's traffic goes through a satellite {{alt}} km up. Treat each hop as a straight {{alt}} km up or down: a request goes up to the satellite and down to the ground station, and the reply comes back the same way. Light travels 300,000 km per second. Ignoring processing time, what is the minimum round-trip time, in milliseconds?
feedback_template: A request and its reply cross four hops (up, down, up, down), so the signal travels 4 × {{alt}} = {{dist}} km. Light covers 300 km per millisecond, so that takes {{expected}} ms. At geostationary height, about 36,000 km, that is nearly half a second before any processing, which is why GEO links feel sluggish and LEO links don't.

question: NPC: How does one access point grow into a campus network?
intro: One access point on a café wall looks after itself. Forty of them across three buildings are a different job, because a laptop carried from one building to the next shouldn't notice it has changed access points. It all starts with how each radio names itself on the air.

beats.say: One AP radio and its clients form a **basic service set** (BSS).
The **SSID** is the network name; the **BSSID** is that radio's MAC address.
Several APs sharing one SSID and wired network form an **extended service set** (ESS).
A laptop can **roam** from one AP to the next.

check.prompt: A dual-band AP broadcasts the SSID Silverkeep on its 2.4 GHz radio and on its 5 GHz radio. How many BSSIDs does it advertise?
check.answer: Two: each radio forms its own BSS
wrong: One, because the SSID is the same
None: only a controller has a BSSID
check.why: A BSS is one radio's cell, and each has its own BSSID, even when both carry the same SSID. A client sees two entries with one name and picks the radio that suits it.

That is fine for two APs and painful for two hundred.
A **lightweight** AP is almost blank on its own.

check.prompt: A WLC pushes a new guest SSID to 200 lightweight APs at once. What would the same change take with 200 autonomous APs?
check.answer: Configuring the SSID on each AP separately
wrong: Nothing: autonomous APs copy settings from each other
Rebooting each AP so it fetches the SSID itself
check.why: Autonomous APs have no controller to take settings from, so every change is made on every AP, by hand or by a script that visits each one. That is the work a controller removes.

beats.say: The controller runs the fleet: SSIDs, security, channels, power and firmware in one place.
It can be an appliance, a virtual machine or a cloud service.
An **extender**, or repeater, rebroadcasts an AP's signal into a dead spot, but a single-radio one halves the throughput behind it.

The AP raises its power to feed it

feedback: Autonomous APs carry their full configuration and are managed one at a time, which suits a handful of APs. Lightweight APs join a wireless LAN controller, which hands firmware, SSIDs, security and RF plans to the whole fleet from one place.

question: The Gilded Tankard, in the United States, wants 6 GHz Wi-Fi in its beer garden, from an AP on an outdoor pole. Which AP is allowed there?
correct: A standard-power AP that gets its channels from an AFC service
incorrect: A low-power indoor AP, mounted under the eaves out of the rain
A low-power indoor AP, fitted with a higher-gain external antenna
A Wi-Fi 6 outdoor AP, with its radio set to the 6 GHz band
feedback: Outdoor 6 GHz in the US needs a standard-power AP, which checks with an automated frequency coordination (AFC) service for the channels and power allowed at its location. Low-power indoor APs are for indoor use only, however sheltered they are, and they can't take an external antenna either. A Wi-Fi 6 radio can't use 6 GHz at all; that takes Wi-Fi 6E or 7.

question: Ravenshade Academy links its admin building (A) to three outlying buildings (B, C and D) by wireless, as drawn. Which design matches the drawing?
correct: Point-to-multipoint, with a sector or omni antenna at A
incorrect: Point-to-point, with one narrow dish at A aimed at all three
Mesh, with B, C and D relaying traffic for each other
Point-to-multipoint, with a narrow dish at A aimed only at B
feedback: One hub (A) talking to several remote sites (B, C and D), with no links among them, is point-to-multipoint: the hub uses a wide sector or omni antenna, and each remote aims a directional antenna back at it. One narrow dish can cover only one far site, which would make a single point-to-point link. A mesh would show the outlying buildings relaying to each other, and the drawing has no such links.

question: Which wireless hardware choices are sound?
correct: A ceiling-mounted omnidirectional AP in the middle of an open-plan office
A pair of dishes aimed at each other for a point-to-point link between buildings
An extender for a small dead spot that no cable can reach, accepting lower speed there
incorrect: A directional antenna, chosen because it adds energy to the AP's signal
An omnidirectional antenna at each end of a 2 km building-to-building link
A single-radio extender, expected to give the same speed behind it as in front
feedback: An omni in the middle of a ceiling covers the room around it, and a pair of dishes aimed at each other focuses energy along a building-to-building link. An extender is a fair fix for a small dead spot, as long as you accept that relaying cuts its throughput. Directional antennas don't add energy, they focus it; and omnis at both ends of a 2 km link would send most of their energy away from the far end. A single-radio extender halves the throughput behind it, so the speed there cannot match the speed in front.

question: Arrange how a new lightweight AP goes from power-on to serving clients.
items: The AP boots and requests an IP address by DHCP
The AP learns a controller's address from DHCP or DNS
The AP joins the controller over a CAPWAP tunnel
The controller sends the AP firmware and its configuration
The AP starts broadcasting the SSIDs it was given
feedback: Nothing works without an address, so DHCP comes first, and the same DHCP reply (or a DNS lookup) tells the AP where its controller is. It then joins over CAPWAP, takes the controller's firmware and settings, and only then knows which SSIDs to broadcast.

question: NPC: Who gets onto your Wi-Fi, and who can read it?
intro: Wi-Fi doesn't stop at the walls: anyone in the parking lot with a laptop can capture the frames you send. So protection has to come from encryption, and from deciding who's allowed to join at all. The encryption has been rebuilt more than once since its first version was broken, and the first rebuild was only a stopgap.

beats.say: **WPA** was a stopgap after the original WEP encryption was broken.
It used **TKIP**, the Temporal Key Integrity Protocol, which wraps the old RC4 cipher with per-packet keys.
**WPA2** made **AES**, the Advanced Encryption Standard, mandatory.
AES runs in a mode called **CCMP**.

steps.say: **WPA** was a stopgap after the original WEP encryption was broken. It used **TKIP**, the Temporal Key Integrity Protocol, which wraps the old RC4 cipher with per-packet keys. **WPA2** made **AES**, the Advanced Encryption Standard, mandatory. AES runs in a mode called **CCMP**.

beats.say: TKIP is now deprecated. Newer standards refuse fast rates with it, so such a client drops to old 54 Mbps speeds.
In Windows output, `CCMP` means AES. `TKIP` means the old cipher.
**WPA3** keeps AES and fixes how a shared passphrase is used.

steps.say: TKIP is now deprecated. Newer standards refuse fast rates with it, so such a client drops to old 54 Mbps speeds. In Windows output, `CCMP` means AES. `TKIP` means the old cipher. **WPA3** keeps AES and fixes how a shared passphrase is used.

beats.say: Its personal mode uses **SAE**, Simultaneous Authentication of Equals, so a captured handshake can't be used to guess the passphrase offline.
WPA3 also requires **Protected Management Frames** (PMF), which block forged disconnect messages.
The 6 GHz band allows no WPA2: a secured 6 GHz SSID must use WPA3.

check.why: Personal mode has one secret for everyone, so the only way to lock one person out is to change it for all. Disabling one account is the Enterprise way, which is why larger sites use 802.1X.

wrong: The guest VLAN blocks all HTTPS by design

question: Match each Wi-Fi security mechanism to what it does.

pairs.definition: Wraps the old RC4 cipher with per-packet keys; now deprecated
Encrypts traffic with AES; mandatory since WPA2
Lets a shared passphrase resist offline guessing in WPA3
Signs each user in with their own credentials via RADIUS
Blocks forged disconnect and other management frames

feedback: TKIP was WPA's interim fix, built on RC4 and now deprecated; CCMP is the AES-based protection WPA2 made mandatory and WPA3 keeps. SAE replaces WPA2's passphrase exchange in WPA3-Personal, and PMF, which WPA3 requires, protects management frames. 802.1X is the Enterprise sign-in, checked by RADIUS.

question: A Wi-Fi 6 laptop at Silverkeep never connects faster than 54 Mbps, however close it sits to the AP. Brom suspects a weak antenna. Which change fixes both the speed and the security?
code:
Authentication     : WPA2-Personal
Cipher             : TKIP
Receive rate (Mbps): 54
correct: Set the SSID to use AES (CCMP) only, dropping TKIP
incorrect: Replace the AP's antennas with higher-gain models
Keep TKIP but lengthen the passphrase to 20 characters
Move the SSID back to WPA, which TKIP was designed for
feedback: TKIP is the clue: newer Wi-Fi standards refuse their fast rates with TKIP, so the client falls back to old 54 Mbps speeds, and TKIP's RC4 base is deprecated as well. Setting the SSID to AES (CCMP) only fixes both. Brom's antenna theory can't explain a ceiling that holds right next to the AP; a longer passphrase strengthens the key but not the cipher; and going back to WPA is a step backward.

question: In WPA3-{{1}} mode everyone shares one passphrase, protected by the SAE handshake. In WPA3-{{2}} mode each user signs in through 802.1X, and a {{3}} server checks their credentials.
feedback: Personal mode uses one shared passphrase (with SAE in WPA3, a pre-shared key in WPA2). Enterprise mode uses 802.1X: each user's own credentials, checked by RADIUS, so one person can be cut off without changing anything for everyone else.

question: Which statements about WPA3 are correct?
correct: Its personal mode uses SAE, so a captured handshake can't be cracked offline
A secured 6 GHz SSID must use it rather than WPA2
incorrect: It drops Enterprise mode, so every network uses a passphrase
Its transition mode lets WPA2 clients join a 6 GHz SSID
It leaves Protected Management Frames optional
feedback: WPA3 swaps the passphrase exchange for SAE so a captured handshake gives an attacker nothing to test guesses against, and it is the only option for a secured 6 GHz SSID. It also requires PMF, so they are not optional, and it still has an Enterprise mode with 802.1X. Transition mode, which admits WPA2 clients, is allowed only in 2.4 and 5 GHz.

question: Arrange what happens when a guest connects to the Gilded Tankard's guest Wi-Fi, which uses a captive portal.
items: The guest's phone associates with the guest SSID
DHCP gives the phone an address on the guest VLAN
The phone's first web request is redirected to the portal page
The guest accepts the terms of use on the portal
The controller lets the phone's MAC address through to the internet
feedback: The phone must join the SSID before it can ask DHCP for an address, and it needs an address before it can send a web request for the network to redirect. The portal page collects the guest's acceptance, and only then does the controller authorize the device, usually by its MAC address, for internet access.

question: The Gilded Tankard's tills (point-of-sale terminals) sit on VLAN 10. Lyra must make sure guests on the new guest Wi-Fi can't reach them. Which control does that?
correct: Map the guest SSID to its own VLAN, firewalled to internet only
incorrect: Put a captive portal with terms of use in front of the guest SSID
Hide the tills' SSID so it never appears in a guest's network list
Secure the guest SSID with WPA3-Personal and a printed passphrase
feedback: Separation is a routing and filtering job: a guest VLAN whose firewall rules permit only internet traffic can't reach VLAN 10, however a guest behaves. A captive portal decides who gets on, not where they can go. Hiding an SSID hides only a name, and WPA3 encrypts guest traffic without limiting where it may go.

question:
Aria's site survey of the Gilded Tankard lists each AP's clients and neighbors, as shown. Policy:
1. Band: the highest band that every client on that AP supports.
2. Channel: one that overlaps no neighboring AP on the same band and is not a DFS channel where radar was logged. In 2.4 GHz use only 1, 6 or 11.
3. Security: WPA3 if every client supports it; WPA2/WPA3 transition if the clients are mixed; WPA2 (AES) if no client supports WPA3. No TKIP.
Choose each AP's band, channel and security.
rows: Card readers: 2.4 GHz only, WPA2 only. Neighbors on 1 and 11.
Wi-Fi 6 phones (WPA3) and Wi-Fi 5 tablets (WPA2 only). Neighbor on 36; radar logged on 52.
Wi-Fi 6E laptops only, all WPA3. No 6 GHz neighbors.
feedback: AP-1's card readers know only 2.4 GHz and WPA2, so it stays on 2.4 GHz with WPA2 (AES); with neighbors on 1 and 11, channel 6 is the one clear choice left, and 3 would overlap both 1 and 6. AP-2's tablets are Wi-Fi 5, so 5 GHz is the highest band everyone shares; 36 is taken and 52 is a DFS channel where radar was logged, leaving 149, and WPA2-only tablets beside WPA3 phones call for transition mode. AP-3's Wi-Fi 6E laptops can use 6 GHz, which accepts only WPA3 anyway. TKIP is never the answer.

question: NPC: Where does all of a building's cabling end up?
intro: I'm Ada, the Chief Artificer. Lift a ceiling tile in any office and you'll find bundles of cable, each one run somewhere on purpose. When a desk loses its connection, you need to know which room its cable runs back to, and whether the fault is even yours to fix. That second question is settled where the carrier's line enters the building.

Faults beyond it are the carrier's to fix.
It usually sits in the **main distribution frame** (MDF): the building's central wiring room.
Each floor gets an **intermediate distribution frame** (IDF): a closet of access switches.

feedback: Follow the path: the carrier hands off at the demarc, usually in the MDF beside the core gear; backbone fiber runs from the MDF's fiber distribution panel to each IDF, where access switches and patch panels serve the desks. The meet-me room is a colocation facility's meeting point, where tenants and carriers cross-connect.

question: Arrange the path a user's traffic takes from their desk out to the carrier.
items: The wall jack at the user's desk
The patch panel in the floor's IDF
The access switch in the IDF
Backbone fiber, through fiber distribution panels, to the MDF
The core switch and edge router in the MDF
The demarcation point, where the carrier's circuit begins
feedback: Horizontal cable runs from the wall jack to the IDF's patch panel, and a patch cord takes the signal to the access switch. The switch's uplink rides the backbone fiber, landing on a fiber distribution panel at each end, to the MDF's core switch and edge router, which meets the carrier at the demarc.

question: Old Hask is tidying Silverkeep's second-floor IDF. Which practices should he follow?
correct: Label both ends of each cable with the same ID used on its panel port
Bundle cables with hook-and-loop straps rather than tight zip ties
Tag each switch with an asset ID that matches its inventory record
incorrect: Tie power cords tightly alongside the data bundles to save space
Coil the spare cable neatly in front of the switch's air vents
Label only the switch end of each cable and trace the panel end by hand
feedback: Matching labels at both ends and on the panel let anyone trace a run without pulling it, and an asset tag ties each device to its inventory record. Hook-and-loop straps hold a bundle without crushing the cable. Power cords lashed to data cables invite interference, and a coil across a vent starves the switch of air. Labeling only one end leaves someone tracing the other end by hand.

question: During a risky core-switch upgrade at Silverkeep, Aria wants a sure way to reach the switch's CLI even if all of its uplinks go down. Which setup gives her that?
correct: Cable its management port to a separate out-of-band network
incorrect: Enable SSH on the switch's address in the production server VLAN
Patch the management port into a user access switch on the same floor
Add a second IP address to the same uplink interface for admins
feedback: Out-of-band management means a path that doesn't share the production network's fate: a management port on its own network, or a console server, still answers when the uplinks are down. SSH to a production VLAN, a management port patched into the user network, and a second address on the same uplink all ride the links that might fail.

question: On a Linux laptop, Old Hask has cabled a switch's console to the laptop's built-in serial port, /dev/ttyS0. Write the screen command that opens that console at 9600 baud.
correct: screen /dev/ttyS0 9600
sudo screen /dev/ttyS0 9600
feedback: screen takes the serial device first and the speed second: screen /dev/ttyS0 9600. A console opened at the wrong speed shows garbled characters or nothing at all, so match the device's console settings, most often 9600 baud, 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit.

question: In a colocation facility, the neutral space where carriers and tenants link their equipment with cross-connect cables is the ___.
correct: meet-me room
MMR
meet me room
meetme room
feedback: The meet-me room (MMR) is where every carrier in a colo has a presence, so a tenant reaches any of them with one short cross-connect, ordered from the facility, without either side entering the other's cage.

question: NPC: How do you power a rack and keep it running?
intro: A switch can be configured perfectly and still go dark because a breaker tripped down the hall. Power fails in two ways: you ask a circuit for more than it can give, or the utility stops sending any. Both kinds of failure are easier to plan for once you know what feeds the rack.

beats.say: Start with the **power source**: the utility feed, the circuits it arrives on, and their voltage.
Critical racks get two independent feeds, A and B, so one failed circuit leaves the other.

steps.say: Start with the **power source**: the utility feed, the circuits it arrives on, and their voltage. Critical racks get two independent feeds, A and B, so one failed circuit leaves the other.

beats.say: **Power load** is what the equipment draws. Add up the watts, then divide by the circuit's voltage to get amps.
In the US, a load that runs continuously is kept to 80% of the breaker's rating.

beats.code:
2 switches 150 W = 300 W
4 servers  400 W = 1,600 W
total = 1,900 W
1,900 W / 120 V ~ 15.8 A
20 A x 80% = 16 A (fits)

wrong: Yes: 18.3 A is still under the 20 A breaker

check.why: 2,200 W divided by 120 V is about 18.3 A. That is under the breaker's 20 A, but over the 16 A that 80% allows for a continuous load, so the server needs another circuit.

A **metered** PDU shows the load; a **switched** PDU can turn outlets off and on remotely.
A PDU stores no energy: when its feed fails, so does everything plugged into it.

It keeps the load up for minutes only.

feedback_template: The circuit's full rating is {{b}} A × {{v}} V = {{va}} W, and 80% of that is {{cap}} W. The rack already uses {{load}} W, which leaves {{expected}} W. Going past the 80% line is how a rack that ran fine for months trips its breaker on a busy day.

question: Aria finds that every dual-power-supply server in a Silverkeep rack has both supplies plugged into PDU-A, while PDU-B, on a separate circuit, sits empty. What is the risk?
correct: Losing PDU-A's feed drops every server; move one supply of each to PDU-B
incorrect: Two supplies on one PDU double each server's draw; spread them to halve it
None: the metered PDU keeps the servers running a while on its reserve
None: if one power supply fails, the other carries the server on PDU-A
feedback: Two power supplies protect against a failed supply, not a failed feed: with both on PDU-A, one tripped breaker takes every server down. Split them, one supply on each PDU, each PDU on its own circuit. A server shares its load across its supplies, so plugging both into one PDU doubles nothing, and no PDU, metered or not, stores energy.

question: During an outage, a {{1}} carries the load on batteries for minutes. A {{2}} can run for hours on fuel but needs seconds to start, and an automatic {{3}} switch moves the load onto it once it is ready.
feedback: The UPS bridges the gap instantly from its batteries; the generator supplies the long haul but must start and come up to speed first; and the automatic transfer switch (ATS) moves the load from the utility to the generator, and back when the utility returns.

question: Silverkeep's MDF has a UPS, a generator and an automatic transfer switch. Arrange what happens from the moment utility power fails until the generator stops.
items: Utility power fails
The UPS carries the load on its batteries
The generator starts and comes up to speed
The ATS transfers the load to the generator
Utility power returns, and the ATS transfers the load back
The generator runs a cool-down and shuts off
feedback: The UPS reacts first because it needs no start-up; the generator takes several seconds to reach speed, and only then does the ATS move the load onto it. When the utility comes back and holds steady, the ATS moves the load back, and the generator idles to cool down before it stops.

question: A UPS's batteries store {{wh}} watt-hours of usable energy, and the rack it protects draws {{w}} W. Ignoring losses, for how many minutes can the UPS carry the rack?
feedback_template: Energy divided by load gives the runtime in hours: {{wh}} Wh over {{w}} W, and times 60 that is {{expected}} minutes. Real runtimes are shorter, because the inverter wastes some energy and batteries deliver less under heavy loads, which is why the generator, not the UPS, covers long outages.

intro: A full rack gives off heat like a space heater that never switches off, usually in a room with the door shut. Let the heat build and the switches start raising alarms, but fight it carelessly and you can end up with water beside live equipment. The first step is simply measuring the air in the right place.

A common target, from the cooling engineers' society ASHRAE, is 18 to 27 °C at the intake.
**Humidity** matters both ways: too dry lets static build up; too damp brings condensation and corrosion.

feedback: The switch's ports face the hot aisle, so its intake must be at the other end, the power-supply side, which faces the cold aisle: air goes in there and leaves at the ports. That is port-side exhaust. A port-side intake model would breathe the servers' hot exhaust. Switch fans don't reverse themselves to suit a room, and venting sideways fights the aisle layout.

question: A new rack of AI training servers at Silverkeep will give off far more heat than the room's air conditioning can remove from one rack. Which change adds the cooling capacity it needs?
correct: Liquid cooling, such as a rear-door heat exchanger or cold plates
incorrect: Blanking panels in every empty space, so no cool air is wasted
Extra ceiling exhaust fans, to ventilate the room's hot air out
A lower thermostat setting, so the supply air arrives colder
feedback: Water carries heat far better than air, so a rear-door heat exchanger or cold plates on the chips can remove what the room's air can't, at the cost of plumbing and leak risk. Blanking panels and ventilation stop cool air being wasted or stale air lingering, but add no capacity, and colder supply air can't move enough heat when air itself is the bottleneck.

question: Silverkeep is choosing fire suppression for its data hall. Which statements are correct?
correct: A pre-action system keeps water out of its pipes until a detector trips
A clean agent puts out the fire without leaving residue on equipment
incorrect: A wet-pipe system is the best fit for a data hall, as it reacts fastest
A dry-pipe system releases water only after a smoke detector trips
A clean agent should discharge at once, with no warning alarm first
feedback: Pre-action pipes stay dry until a detector opens the valve, and a head must still open, so one fault can't flood the room; clean agents such as FM-200 put the fire out and leave nothing behind. Wet-pipe reacts fast but puts water on live gear at the first open head. A dry-pipe valve opens when a head opens and the air pressure drops, not on a detector. A clean agent sounds an alarm first so people can get out.

question: Camera footage shows a visitor slipping into Silverkeep's data hall behind an employee, on a single badge swipe. Lyra must stop this tailgating. Which control most directly prevents it?
correct: An access control vestibule with interlocked doors
incorrect: A biometric reader in place of the badge reader on that door
More cameras, covering the door from inside and out
Badge readers that log every entry for later review
feedback: A vestibule's two doors never open together, so each authorization admits one person and a follower is caught between the doors. A biometric reader proves who opened the door, but the visitor can still walk in behind them, and cameras and logs record tailgating rather than stopping it.

question: Match each physical security control to what it adds.

pairs.definition: Admits one person per authorization, stopping tailgating
Deters intruders and records events for later review
Unlocks doors and logs entries, but can be lost or lent
Verifies a body trait that can't be handed to someone
Keeps hands off a device even inside a shared room

feedback: Each control covers a gap in another: cards log who entered but can be lent, so biometrics tie entry to a body; vestibules stop the follower that a card or a fingerprint can't; cameras deter and record but stop no one; and a locked rack protects gear from people who are allowed in the room.

question: Old Hask is running new fiber in Silverkeep's MDF. Which actions follow good safety practice?
correct: Wear safety glasses while cleaving and splicing the fiber
Keep the aisle and exit route clear of cable reels and boxes
Check where the first-aid kit and AED are before starting
incorrect: Look into a fiber end to check whether it carries light
Wear an ESD strap to protect yourself from the fiber's laser
Press the EPO to restart a frozen switch quickly
Finish the splice before leaving, since the clean-agent alarm sounds well ahead of discharge
feedback: Glasses protect against glass shards, clear routes keep the room escapable and accessible, and knowing where the first-aid kit and AED are saves minutes. Fiber may carry invisible laser light, so check it with a power meter or viewer and not your eye, and an ESD strap protects the equipment from static but does nothing against a laser. The EPO cuts power to the whole room, which is for fire or shock and not for one frozen switch. The clean-agent alarm sounds first so that people can get out, so leave at once when it sounds.

question: Captain Doran Kell is choosing a room for a new IDF on Silverkeep's third floor. Which room is the best fit?
correct: A central room with cooling, a lockable door and space behind the rack
incorrect: A janitor's closet, beside the floor's mop sink and water heater
An unlocked alcove in the open-plan area, right beside the busiest desks
A basement room under the water main, so every floor can share one IDF
feedback: An IDF wants a central location, to keep every horizontal run within reach, plus cooling, a lock and clearance to work. A janitor's closet puts water beside live gear; an open alcove fails the lockable test; and a basement room under a water main is a flood risk, and too far from the third floor's desks for copper.

question: Ravenshade Academy wants Wi-Fi across an outdoor quad lined with light poles, but only one pole has a network cable. If one pole's link fails, coverage must route around it. Which design fits?
correct: Mesh APs on the poles, relaying to each other and back to the cabled one
incorrect: A chain of range extenders, each one repeating the one before it
Point-to-point bridges from the cabled pole out to each of the others
Autonomous APs on every pole, each broadcasting its own SSID
feedback: Mesh fits: the poles' APs relay traffic over the air to the one with a cable, and if one link fails the others find another path. A chain of extenders cuts throughput at every hop and breaks at its weakest link. Bridges from the cabled pole give every other pole one path only, and autonomous APs on uncabled poles have nothing to connect back to.

question: The Gilded Tankard's new Wi-Fi 6E APs will carry its guest network on 6 GHz too. Guests should join without a passphrase and then accept the terms on a captive portal. How should the 6 GHz guest SSID be secured?
correct: Enhanced Open, which encrypts each guest without a passphrase
incorrect: Open with no encryption, since the captive portal protects guests
WPA2-Personal, with the passphrase printed on the portal page
WPA2/WPA3 transition mode, so older phones can join too
feedback: 6 GHz admits only WPA3 or Enhanced Open, so the old open-plus-portal design isn't allowed there, and WPA2 and transition mode are out as well. Enhanced Open encrypts each guest's traffic with no passphrase, and the captive portal still collects the terms. A portal on its own encrypts nothing.

question: A US standard-power 6 GHz AP may transmit only on the channels, and at the power, that an ___ service allows at its location.
correct: AFC
automated frequency coordination
feedback: Automated frequency coordination (AFC) protects licensed microwave links that also use 6 GHz: the standard-power AP reports where it is, and the AFC service answers with the channels and power allowed there. Low-power indoor APs skip AFC, which is why they are held to indoor use and lower power.

question: Silverkeep is choosing a colocation facility in a new European country. Which are regional considerations to weigh?
correct: Data-residency laws on where customer records may be stored
The local climate, which drives the facility's cooling cost
The region's history of floods and earthquakes
incorrect: Mains power of 120 V at 60 Hz, so the gear's power supplies need no check
Rack units, which are 2 inches tall in Europe instead of 1.75
Whether the facility has an access control vestibule
Whether each cage has its own console server
feedback: Law, climate and natural hazards all change with the region: records may have to stay in the country, a hot climate costs more to cool, and flood or quake risk shapes the choice. Mains power in Europe is 230 V at 50 Hz, so the gear's power supplies must accept it, and 120 V at 60 Hz does not apply there. A rack unit is 1.75 inches (44.45 mm) everywhere, and a vestibule or console server is a feature of one facility and not of a region.
